clinical_category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control

semantic_correction.stem: A hospital measures ATP bioluminescence on selected environmental surfaces before and after cleaning. What does this method assess?

options.A: Residual organic material that can provide objective feedback about cleaning effectiveness.
options.B: The exact pathogen species remaining on each sampled surface after cleaning.
options.C: Whether the sampled surface has achieved microbiologic sterility after cleaning.
options.D: Whether routine environmental cleaning can be omitted when ATP readings are low.

semantic_correction.rationale: CDC describes ATP bioluminescence as a method in which detection of ATP indicates that organic microbial or biologic material is present on a surface. Comparing measurements before and after cleaning can provide objective feedback about the effectiveness of the cleaning procedure. CDC also lists important limitations, including low sensitivity and specificity and no standardized threshold that declares a surface 'safe.' ATP testing therefore does not identify an exact pathogen species, establish sterility, or replace environmental cleaning.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Interpret ATP bioluminescence as an objective measure of residual organic material used to assess cleaning effectiveness, not as a pathogen-identification or sterility test.
semantic_correction.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
semantic_correction.source_document_title: Environmental Cleaning Procedures — Methods for Assessment of Cleaning and Cleanliness

semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: ATP bioluminescence detects residual organic microbial or biologic material and can provide objective before/after feedback about cleaning effectiveness; it has limited sensitivity/specificity and no standardized threshold for declaring a surface safe.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: shortened the uniquely long correct answer, rebuilt distractors as parallel interpretations of ATP testing, and retained CDC's explicit limitations so the item does not overstate ATP as a pathogen-identification or sterility method.

audit_findings_append.finding: The original answer was uniquely longest. The revised item retains the exact CDC use and limitations of ATP testing while making all choices comparable interpretations of the measurement.

option_audit.A: Correct. CDC states that ATP indicates residual organic material and before/after testing can assess cleaning effectiveness.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. ATP bioluminescence does not identify the exact pathogen species; targeted culture may identify specific bacteria.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. ATP results do not prove sterility, and CDC notes there is no standardized threshold declaring a surface safe.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. ATP monitoring assesses cleaning effectiveness; it does not replace the cleaning process itself.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone describes the CDC-defined information provided by ATP bioluminescence without adding unsupported diagnostic or sterility claims.
cueing_check: All four options are interpretations of ATP monitoring with comparable length and specificity; no absolute-word or unique-length cue identifies A.
